questions.q: What keyword must appear on a T-SQL output parameter, in BOTH the procedure definition and the call?
options: OUTPUT
OUT
RETURN
RESULT
questions.explain: T-SQL requires OUTPUT on the parameter in CREATE PROCEDURE and again at the EXEC call site; forgetting it at the call site silently fails to populate the variable.

questions.q: What are PL/SQL's three parameter directions, declared directly in the parameter list?
options: IN, OUT, and IN OUT
INPUT, OUTPUT, and BOTH
READ, WRITE, and READWRITE
PL/SQL has no concept of parameter direction
questions.explain: PL/SQL parameters declare IN (read-only, default), OUT (write-only), or IN OUT (both) explicitly as part of the parameter declaration.

questions.q: What happens in T-SQL if you forget the OUTPUT keyword at the call site (EXEC proc @p = @var) when the parameter was defined as OUTPUT?
options: The statement runs without erroring, but the variable is silently not populated with the result
SQL Server throws a compile error immediately
The procedure refuses to execute at all
T-SQL automatically adds OUTPUT for you
questions.explain: This is a genuinely confusing T-SQL gotcha — the EXEC statement succeeds, it just doesn't actually assign the output value back to your variable.

questions.q: How does PL/SQL's OUT parameter differ from T-SQL's OUTPUT parameter in terms of being write-only?
options: PL/SQL's OUT is properly write-only, while T-SQL's OUTPUT parameter can also receive an input value, making it closer to PL/SQL's IN OUT
They behave identically in every respect
T-SQL's OUTPUT is write-only and PL/SQL's OUT can receive input
Neither platform allows a parameter to both receive input and return output
questions.explain: T-SQL only has two parameter states (normal or OUTPUT), and its OUTPUT parameter can carry an input value in too — unlike PL/SQL's properly write-only OUT, which maps more precisely to PL/SQL's own IN OUT.

questions.q: What are two valid ways to call a PL/SQL procedure directly (outside of a client API)?
options: Call it directly, e.g. GetProductPrice(707, v_price); or wrap it in an anonymous block with BEGIN ... END;
Only CALL GetProductPrice(...) is valid, nothing else
PL/SQL procedures cannot be called manually at all
Only EXEC GetProductPrice(...) is valid
questions.explain: PL/SQL procedures can be invoked as a standalone statement or from within a BEGIN...END anonymous block, unlike T-SQL which always uses EXEC.
